1.pericope_label: When I would have healed Israel, then the iniquity of Ephraim was discovered, and the wickedness of Samaria: for they commit falsehood
debates: Why the wickedness appeared just then
What it is that they failed to consider
outliers: Gill insists the healing is neither a wish nor an attempt but an actual and political healing, the restoring of the civil state under Jeroboam the son of Joash, where Henry takes it of a reformation offered and Ellicott of a respite from an invading enemy
Calvin holds that vice appears precisely when God applies the remedy, so that a people left untried rest quietly in their own dregs and look better than they are
themes: A physician finding an older disease under the new
A wound probed until it is found to touch the vitals
A stream swelling higher for being dammed
A God imagined asleep in heaven

3.pericope_label: They make the king glad with their wickedness, and the princes with their lies
outliers: Calvin refuses the plea that the people were only obeying their king, and argues from the suddenness of the collapse that the wickedness had been concocted inwardly already and needed only an occasion
Clarke reports a paraphrase that works the oven out politically, the kingdom being the oven the king himself set alight, where Ellicott and Calvin both take the heat for the burning of appetite
themes: A king glad to hear that one altar is as good as another
A whole people who needed only an occasion
A baker feeding a smouldering fire all night
Bread left in an oven that consumed it

5.pericope_label: In the day of our king the princes have made him sick with bottles of wine; he stretched out his hand with scorners
debates: What the day of the king is
Whose plot the oven now figures
outliers: Ellicott follows the ancient versions and a different pointing to read that the princes began the day of the king with the glowing of wine, an early hour signifying monstrous excess, and calls the common English rendering inaccurate
Calvin insists the oven means something different here from what it meant three verses earlier, lust there and concealed plotting here, and says interpreters pass the change over heedlessly
themes: A coronation day that should have been a thanksgiving
A fire banked at night so the baker can sleep
Four kings dead by the hands of their successors
A body with the head taken away

8.pericope_label: Ephraim, he hath mixed himself among the people; Ephraim is a cake not turned
outliers: Ellicott takes the unturned cake for ruin by a foreign fire, burnt to a cinder on one side and left unfit for food on the other, where Calvin, Henry and Wesley all take it for inconstancy, a thing neither one thing nor the other
Gill reports and sets aside a reading that makes the mixing a punishment already inflicted, the people carried captive among the nations, rather than a sin they had committed
themes: A cake baked on one side and raw on the other
A people begging help from those who ate them
Grey hairs sprinkled on a kingdom
A man calling in doctors to cure old age

10.pericope_label: And the pride of Israel testifieth to his face: and they do not return to the Lord their God, nor seek him for all this
debates: Whether the word means testify or humble
Which reign the errand belongs to
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject two readings of the dove, that it has lost its resting place and flutters about, and that it flies into the net while escaping a hawk, keeping only the third, that it fails to see the net while searching for food
Ellicott fixes the verse on a particular usurper who bought recognition from Assyria while secretly courting Egypt, and notes that many commentators refer it to an earlier reign instead
themes: Pride standing as a witness for the prosecution
A dove pecking scattered grain over a spread net
Two rival courts and one small kingdom
A simplicity that is only folly

12.pericope_label: When they shall go, I will spread my net upon them; I will bring them down as the fowls of the heaven; I will chastise them, as their congregation hath heard
debates: Whether the redeeming is past or wished
outliers: Calvin defends the past tense against both a question, shall I redeem them, and a wish, though I would have redeemed them, where Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both take the verb as voluntative, I would fain redeem them
Clarke reports a rendering that turns the last clause round, so that God chastises them when they hearken to their assembly, that is, when they take the counsel of their elders to go down to Egypt
themes: A net spread where the bird means to land
Counsels that no Spirit presides over
A flight allowed to reach the clouds and then stopped
Kindness answered with lies

14.pericope_label: And they have not cried unto me with their heart, when they howled upon their beds: they assemble themselves for corn and wine, and they rebel against me
debates: What the howling on the beds is
What the binding of the arms means
outliers: Ellicott reports a reading drawn from the ancient version and some manuscripts by which they cut themselves rather than assemble themselves, and thinks it not improbably the right one

Calvin rejects both to chastise and to instruct for the first verb of the last verse and takes it of binding, comparing the nerves that hold an arm together, so that God is a surgeon here and not a teacher
themes: A howl on a bed that never became a prayer
A crowd gathered for corn rather than for God
An arm set and swathed by the hand it strikes at
Strength given and turned against the giver

16.pericope_label: They return, but not to the most High: they are like a deceitful bow: their princes shall fall by the sword for the rage of their tongue
debates: Whether the return is to God or upward
outliers: Clarke explains the figure from the eastern bow, which rests in a curve and must be bent the opposite way to be strung, and which recoils on the archer if he wants the skill; he says he has been in that danger himself, and that for want of this knowledge no commentator has hit the meaning
Ellicott makes the raving of the tongue the boasting of an Egyptian friendship, so that the derision falls in the very country whose favour was boasted
themes: A bow that springs back on the man who bends it
An arrow aimed at a mark it will never reach
A return that goes everywhere but upward
Boasts repeated back as mockery
